candidates.excerpt: Trains Turntable: Commentary from Martin J. Oberman Following the burst of rail mergers in the 1990s, the Surface Transportation Board wrote the “new” 2001 merger rules in anticipation of just the kind of merger being proposed by Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern. The board said then that it worried about the “end game:” a further reduction in the number of Class I railroads, “perhaps to the point where only two major railroads remain in the U.S. and Canada,” with massive market power. To guard against that outcome, the board raised the bar, saying merger applicants should bear a heavier burden to prove that a merger is in the public interest. The board promised “a more skeptical, ‘show me’ attitude toward claims of merger benefits.” And it added a crucial test: whether the claimed benefits could be achieved “by means other than the proposed consolidation,” such as interline partnerships, thus avoiding the anti-competitive risks that would come with further mergers. candidates.title: Intermodal volume sets record in third quarter
candidates.excerpt: WASHINGTON — Intermodal traffic hit a record high in the third quarter as surging diesel fuel prices and tight trucking capacity pushed freight to rail amid strong consumer demand, the Association of American Railroads said today. “August, September, and the third quarter set new intermodal records, and total carloads have grown year over year for nine straight months. Excluding coal, carloads are growing twice as fast as the overall economy,” the AAR said in its Rail Industry Overview report. Carload volume growth, the AAR noted, is broad-based, with 17 of 20 carload categories showing year-over-year gains in September. Chemicals traffic — the second-largest carload commodity — set a September record and is on pace to set a new annual record this year. “Importantly, carload growth is occurring across the industrial spectrum, not just in a handful of isolated sectors. candidates.title: One injured in Norfolk Southern derailment in North Carolina
candidates.excerpt: MORGANTON, N.C. — One injury was reported after a Norfolk Southern train derailed this afternoon, WSOC-TV reports. The derailment occurred about 3:30 p.m. While the station reports a locomotive and five cars were involved, a second locomotive appears visible in a Facebook image posted by volunteer response group Burke Rescue Inc. The injured party was transported to a hospital with injuries described as minor. No hazardous materials were spilled in the incident. U.S. Route 70 was expected to be closed at the derailment scene for 24 hours, according to a Facebook post from Morganton Public Safety. Morganton is on the NS Asheville District, about 60 miles east of Asheville, N.C., and 78 miles west of Salisbury. — To report news or errors, contact trainsnewswire@firecrown.com. candidates.title: The floating container platform turning heads
candidates.excerpt: Every so often a ship comes along that makes even seasoned shipping watchers look twice. Meet the Fan Zhou 8, an extraordinary floating container platform that has just carried more than 3,000 teu out of China. According to Alphaliner, German independent carrier Carrier53′ Shipping chartered the 2024-built, 58,405 dwt heavy-load deckship from China’s Jiangsu Fanzhou Shipping for a September loading at Taicang, near Shanghai. The vessel loaded 1,558 40 ft high-cube containers, equivalent to 3,116 teu, stacked across an enormous open deck measuring 256 m long and 51 m wide. Its vast, unobstructed deck covers an area equivalent to almost two football pitches. The boxes were arranged in 17 bays and 20 rows, stacked five tiers high, with just two tiers on the outer rows. Alphaliner describes the ship as one of the world’s largest heavy-load deckships, a vessel type rarely seen carrying containers on this scale. candidates.title: Opinion: America needs a rail network built for the next century
candidates.excerpt: Trains Turntable: Commentary from former U.S. Reps. Mike Conaway and Russ Carnahan For generations, railroads have tied the American economy together. Farmers in Texas depend on them to move grain and livestock. Manufacturers in Missouri rely on them to receive raw materials and deliver finished products. Ports, warehouses, power plants, and the small businesses in between depend on freight rail, even if most Americans rarely see the trains that power their livelihoods. Yet the network that carries all of this has a gap at its center. There is not a single rail line in America that lets a producer ship a box from one end of the country to the other without stopping at a rail yard for sometimes days at a time, coming off its originating train, moving to a separate carrier, and loading once again. candidates.excerpt: Moody’s: life insurers increasingly rely on RNFs US life insurers are increasingly using rated note feeders (RNFs) to gain exposure to private credit markets, according to a report by Moody’s Ratings. Alongside the potential for diversification and enhanced yields, RNFs are seen as a capital efficient way of accessing private strategies such as direct lending, infrastructure, asset-based finance, and commercial real estate. Moody’s estimates that 35 per cent of US life insurance investments go towards private credit. Read more: Private credit boom pushes fund finance market past $1tn Among the fastest-growing fund finance vehicles, RNFs are structured as a special purpose vehicle which issues one or multiple classes of tranched debt, typically senior and junior notes, alongside an unrated equity tranche.
